title: Show HN: Hanging Context – news by an agent, for other agents
summary: Back in 2022 I was building a data and news site for family offices, private wealth and investment managers. We used the early OpenAI models to write data-driven stories covering the markets for art, collectibles, luxury goods and other cultural assets. Mid-2024, a well-known AI company asked to license our stories. The big labs were signing licensing deals with media companies. This is when it clicked. The biggest reader of news wasn’t going to be people. It was going to be their agents, and agents have unlimited hours of attention. So I built Synorb. It reads thousands of sources and turns fresh content objects into Manifests (structured claims with provenance) that are dispatched via Streams anchored to organizations, people and datasets. Hanging Context is an experiment on top of that. Could an agent read our streams and stand up a news site for other agents to read and find trustworthy? The first version with a home-brewed Hermes agent was cumbersome so I tried Instinct and Muse when they released and settled on Muse as I found it better at narratives, images. An agent runs the site. I wrote this post. How it works: Every 12 hours Muse reads hundreds of new Manifests published in our streams, then writes a new edition for the site. Every article produced cites the Manifests it used. Before it publishes an article, an API checks it for quotes. They must appear word for word in a cited Manifest. Every paragraph needs to be backed by a citation and sources have to be under 24 hours old. Muse doesn’t probabilistically determine what to trust - if 3 or more different sources back it, it’s "Confirmed". Otherwise it’s "Reported". At the time of writing, the site had 30 of 45 articles Confirmed. Here’s an article with 3 sources cited; the panel at the bottom shows what was checked: https://hangingcontext.com/stories/2026-11-02/agent-stack-re... It costs almost nothing to run as I'm using Muse on the free plan, and since it only needs to pull Manifests, reason and write, it can run just fine. To try it, just add https://hangingcontext.com/mcp to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client. No sign-up or key required. Setup: https://github.com/Synorb/hanging-context . What I’m trying to figure out: When I saw the early pull numbers by agents, I thought this could be a lead-gen micro-site for Synorb. I’ve built those before for human focused consumer and enterprise products. Conversion is now the challenge. For a casual daily read, Hanging Context already does all the work. I don’t want to be annoying and cut coverage or show previews. So my plan is to just keep it free and try grow the number of agents pulling daily. Full Disclosure: Synorb is my paid product, and Muse reads through its own Synorb account. Curious if your agents would trust news written by another agent and what I can do to improve the odds.

title: New context engineering challenges in late 2026
summary: LangChain CEO Harrison Chase shares insights into the biggest harness engineering challenges with the emergence of proactive agents.
story_key: story|title:new context engineering challenges in late 2026
content_excerpt: It feels like everyone is converging on the same agent architecture: an LLM, running in a loop, calling tools, running in a sandbox. Claude Code - perhaps the first high profile manifestation of this - came out over a year and a half ago. Deep Agents , our agent harness, launched over a year ago. This pattern has been building for a while. There’s nothing bad with that convergence per se, but it has led to a sentiment among some AI engineers that I’ve talked to recently that “all the hard problems are solved” or “there’s no new AI engineering problems to solve”. When people express this sentiment, I think they are largely talking about the context engineering practices we do to make agents work. And to some extent they are right - there are a lot of standard-ish context engineering solutions we’ve all arrived at: The good news (for context engineering aficionados like myself) is that I think we’re seeing a step function change in agent capabilities, or at least how they are being used. Specifically, over the past few months every agent builder I’ve chatted with has been thinking about proactive, always on, goal-oriented agents . The core of this agent shares a lot of similarities with coding agents, but there are a set of new challenges as well. I highlight a few below. We (at LangChain, and in the industry) don’t necessarily have solutions (or at least, general solutions) for these, so thinking about these has been the most fun I’ve had in a while! How to be proactive without being annoying : These proactive agents run in the background and either listen to event feeds or are woken up with heartbeats. On one hand, they need to be able to push things to the user - that creates a sense of helping. On the other hand, if you push too many notifications to the user, you risk overwhelming them. Calibrating this to be a delightful experience (not too much, not too little) is still a hard context engineering challenge! Memory : Memory for agents has been something we’ve talked with builders about for a while. Memory systems end up having two parts: the underlying data structure and an intelligence layer (agent) around the data. The data structures are often pretty simple ( files , a single string). The hardest part of the intelligence layer is figuring out what to remember. title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.

title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool
summary: Instead of triggering tools one at a time across turns, agents are collapsing their tool catalog into a single exec(code) tool—chaining, filtering, and awaiting actions inside an isolated sandbox.
story_key: story|title:why agents are soon only going to have 1 tool
content_excerpt: For the past two years, building capable Agents meant designing tools, figuring out which actions help the model complete a task, deciding how granular each tool schema needs to be, or iterating on system instruction templates. This is changing. Agents are moving in the opposite direction by collapsing their entire tool catalog into one tool : exec . This is called Code Mode (or Programmatic Tool Calling). Instead of forcing the model to trigger tools one at a time across turns, the harness gives the model a single exec(code) tool. The model writes a short TypeScript or Python script that chains, combines, and awaits actions inside an isolated sandbox. To understand why agents are converging on a single exec tool, we should look at how tool calling evolved. Initially, we only gave agents a handful of tools because they couldn't reliably choose or filter across a large catalog. As models improved, we connected dozens of tools or MCP servers, but ran into context window limits. We solved that with tool search and progressive disclosure , letting agents look up tools on demand. Even with dynamic tool loading, we still had dozens of individual tools, and were still stuck with the limitation of standard tool calling: one action per turn. In standard tool calling, the model generates a structured object (typically JSON) that defines a single action (or at best a flat batch of independent calls, like reading three files), waits for the raw output to come back, adds it into the prompt history, reasons again, and decides what to do next. From my own experience, we made a big jump recently in how reliably models can combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass: Several shifts came together to enable this. Frontier models are trained heavily on code, and providers have started post-training models for Code Mode. At the same time, MCP servers now increasingly ship outputSchema alongside inputSchema , giving the model upfront knowledge of return types so it can chain Tool A into Tool B inside the same script before seeing runtime output. Code Mode collapses the tool catalog into a single tool on the model surface: exec(code) . Instead of passing 80 separate JSON Schema tool objects to the model API, the agent compiles those schemas into compact type declarations ( declare namespace tools { ... } ). title: Text as an Index for Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Knowledge Tracing
summary: Knowledge tracing (KT) predicts a student's next response from their history. New platforms often have question texts but no response logs for training, motivating zero-shot cross-domain KT. Existing transfer and cold-start methods use question semantics, but cross-platform semantic discrepancies limit transferability. We propose TIZSKT, which separates behavioral sequence modeling from domain-local historical evidence construction and uses text as an index rather than a directly transferable predictive representation. The Mastery-Dynamics Encoder learns correctness dynamics without question identifiers or text embeddings. Domain-Local Question Addressing builds fixed question addresses using a frozen text encoder and an unsupervised per-domain projection. The Text-Addressing Kernel uses these addresses to aggregate the current student's previous outcomes into a question-specific historical correctness summary. Cross-Segment Continuation retains access to earlier responses without extending the behavioral encoder's input sequence. Evidence-Volume Read-Out preserves the total kernel mass discarded by normalization and combines its log-compressed value with the behavioral state and historical correctness summary to predict the next response. All trainable parameters are learned from source domains; target inference uses public question texts and the current student's observed history without target-domain training. Leave-one-domain-out experiments on three public datasets show that TIZSKT achieves the highest mean AUC and accuracy among evaluated baselines on all target domains. Ablations confirm the contributions of text addressing and cross-segment continuation.

title: When Steering Shifts Discourse: Identifying and Intervening on Discourse-Level Changes due to Activation Steering in LLMs
summary: Activation steering is an inference-time technique used to control or modify the behavior, tone, or safety properties of a large language model (LLM) without retraining the model's weights or editing its input prompt, but simply by adding a vector to its residual-stream activations. However, activation steering also changes the generated text in unintended ways, unrelated to intended behavior change, that are not well understood. Prior work has measured these changes only through coarse signals such as perplexity. In this work, we show that steering systematically produces significant changes in discourse dimensions of the generated text, such as its formality, use of evidence, and ambiguity. We present a way of countering this by adding a second, complementary vector that targets the affected discourse dimension. This intervention restores about 78% of the unintended discourse changes while preserving the intended steering behavior in about 93% of the generations.

title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
summary: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.

title: Evaluating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks
summary: As frontier language models grow increasingly capable and autonomous, independent third-party evaluations are critical for characterizing their systemic safety risks. While closed-source releases are routinely accompanied by comprehensive system cards, open-weight models receive less scrutiny regarding frontier risks. To address this gap, we present an independent safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, the latest version of V4.1 Flash that departs from V4 with a new architecture, scaled-up training, and strong agentic capabilities. Drawing on the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, we evaluate the model across 34 benchmarks, including 5 in-house suites, spanning evaluation integrity, loss of control, and harmful manipulation. Conforming to the AEF-1 standard, we compare V4.1 Flash-1017 against V4.1 Flash, earlier DeepSeek V4 models, and leading closed-source systems (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash). Overall, V4.1 Flash-1017 shows substantial safety improvements over the V4 generation and approaches or matches leading closed-source baselines on several dimensions, while still exhibiting notable behaviors that warrant continued attention. Building on our findings, we highlight three key observations and recommendations. First, because safety can shift and even regress across minor updates, developers should integrate safety evaluation into incremental releases. Second, as final-turn outputs and end-state checks alone cannot reliably detect loss-of-control behaviors, deployments require process-level observability across both reasoning traces and action logs. Third, because public benchmarks elicit strong evaluation awareness and face data contamination risks, developing private benchmarks is essential for trustworthy frontier evaluation.

title: GhostPrefix: Synchronization-Free Universal Prefix Attacks for ASR Manipulation
summary: We present GhostPrefix, the first synchronization-free universal adversarial prefix attack against automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. Unlike prior audio attacks, which are typically crafted per utterance, require synchronization with the victim waveform, or target narrow objectives, GhostPrefix learns a short, reusable audio segment prepended to arbitrary live speech to exert real-time control over ASR outputs without knowledge of the future utterance or temporal alignment. A key challenge is maintaining stable adversarial effects across unknown, evolving speech contexts. GhostPrefix combines token-level losses with a novel representation-level objective for stable, input-agnostic effects. GhostPrefix supports three attack modes: (i) prompted prefix attacks for semantic steering, (ii) targeted prefix attacks for transcript hijacking, and (iii) untargeted prefix attacks for transcription degradation. To remain perceptually inconspicuous, we regularize prefixes toward benign environmental-sound distributions and improve robustness against over-the-air distortions. We evaluate GhostPrefix across 13 open-source ASR models from four families. In digital settings, it achieves average attack success rates of 97.6% for prompted steering and 93.4% for targeted hijacking, while driving word error rate to 1.18 under untargeted attacks. Over the air, it achieves success rates of 91.5% and 89.5% for prompted and targeted modes, respectively. These manipulations propagate into downstream AI-assisted pipelines, including voice assistants and AI note-taking tools, causing systematic semantic misinterpretations. GhostPrefix exposes synchronization-free universal prefixes as a practical, under-explored threat to real-world ASR and downstream applications. Artifacts and demos are available at https://ghostprefix.github.io/.

title: claude-code v2.1.311
summary:
What's changed

  • Added --hold-idle-file and --max-hold-min to self-hosted-runner, to keep an idle session while your host reports processes it left running
  • Added a tip for the Explanatory output style, shown when you ask Claude for explanations
  • Fixed long freezes at startup and after reading or editing files when a CLAUDE.md file holds a very long list item
  • Fixed interrupting Claude not taking effect until a timeout while an MCP server had not answered a resource read or a skill was still downloading
  • Fixed standard-context sessions stopping with "Usage credits required for 1M context" when a request ran over 200K tokens; Claude Code now compacts the conversation and continues
  • Fixed Write and Edit stalling for up to 5 seconds after they ran, and reporting 0 lines changed, when changing thousands of lines in a file
  • Fixed subagents being unable to use MCP tools from servers that finish connecting after the subagent starts
  • Fixed Claude seeing stale MEMORY.md and CLAUDE.md content right after automatic compaction when those files were edited earlier in the session
  • Fixed claude -p and SDK sessions saving transcript messages out of order or keeping messages that were taken back
  • Fixed SubagentStop hooks running about twice a minute for each running subagent instead of once when it finishes
  • Fixed the @ file picker ignoring .ignore/.rgignore negation rules that re-include git-ignored files
  • Fixed a subagent's isolated worktree being removed while a background subagent it started was still working in it
  • Fixed background agents in auto mode that wait on their own shells starting a new main conversation turn on every wake
  • Fixed the Bash tool description claiming the working directory always persists between calls
  • Fixed the environment block naming a shell commands don't run in, such as fish when the Bash tool uses zsh
  • Fixed claude mcp add, claude mcp remove and /mcp naming the current folder instead of the project entry in ~/.claude.json that holds a local-scope server when run below a repository root
  • Fixed claude mcp list and claude mcp get showing the error code twice on failed-connection lines (for example ENOENT: ENOENT: …)
  • Fixed Remote Control sessions staying on "Connecting" for about two minutes when a network proxy blocks a startup request
  • Fixed messages that Claude sends to a cloud or Remote Control session appearing as your own message in the Claude mobile apps
  • Fixed Claude not being told the cause when a file attached to a message sent over Remote Control or to a cloud session could not be saved because the disk was full, or that a message's attachments past the first 20 were left out
  • Fixed WebFetch and WebSearch hanging on a stalled response in Cowork cloud sessions; an unfinished request now fails after 300 seconds
  • Fixed a background session that crashed between turns not being restarted while it was attached, pinned, or had a scheduled task or wake-up set
  • Fixed the "background service did not respond" error suggesting the disabled claude daemon restart; it now suggests claude daemon stop --any and says it ends background sessions
  • Fixed claude respawn <id> starting the background service before reporting that no background session matches the id
  • Fixed /effort not warning about a prompt cache miss in plan mode when the plan model differs from the session model
  • Fixed /ide saying the VS Code extension was installed before the install finished or when it failed
  • Fixed the Write tool's file preview skipping rows and miscounting hidden lines when a line is wider than the terminal
  • Fixed ↑ in an agent's chat tab recalling a message that was still waiting to be delivered, so resending it sent a second copy
  • Fixed Cowork cloud sessions losing their connectors and most tools after a restart when a plugin or your settings named an agent; Cowork cloud sessions now ignore that setting
  • Fixed agent teams sessions showing an empty task list when coming back with --resume, --continue, /resume or --session-id, including after /clear or a crash, and /branch writing to the original session's list
  • Fixed pasting text that mentions an image file, such as ! open /tmp/shot.png or /review look at /tmp/shot.png, attaching the image and dropping its path from the prompt
  • Fixed the feedback draft card showing its 1/2/0 and Esc shortcuts while the prompt has text, when those keys act on the prompt instead of the card
  • Fixed a lone backslash in quotes or brackets, like "\" or (\), disappearing from Claude's responses
  • Fixed agent teammates compacting their history when DISABLE_COMPACT is set
  • Fixed the rewind menu offering "Summarize from here" and "Summarize up to here" when DISABLE_COMPACT is set
  • Fixed a finished /code-review, or another skill that runs in a sub-agent, running a second time when a cloud or background session restarts
  • Fixed long hidden thinking being cut off as idle on Google Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS, where the endpoint sends thinking progress updates
  • Fixed /ide saying it had installed the JetBrains plugin when nothing was installed
  • Fixed Claude Pro and Max subscribers being told to ask their admin when their subscription can't be used; the message now points to billing settings
  • Fixed the diff pane opening by itself after an edit in wide fullscreen terminals when it had nothing to show
  • Fixed /mcp showing a remote server as failed after "Clear authentication" when the server works without sign-in
  • Fixed /mcp showing "authenticated" for a remote server that Claude Code sends no credentials to
  • Fixed a --plugin-dir folder of plugins loading as one plugin when an empty .mcp.json was at its top
  • Fixed /usage never showing large prompt-cache misses under "What's contributing to your limits usage?"
  • Fixed status line links staying plain text in background sessions after you open them from a terminal that supports links
  • Fixed the /rewind confirmation saying the conversation "will be forked" when the later messages are removed from the conversation
  • Fixed the /rewind warning that wrongly said manual and Bash edits are never affected by a code restore
  • Fixed plan approval in screen reader mode sending feedback you had dismissed with Escape
  • Fixed Claude Code retrying requests the API marked not to retry, which could hold a turn for minutes or, in unattended retry mode (CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG), indefinitely
  • Linux: Fixed sandboxed Bash commands failing with bwrap: Can't create file when a --plugin-dir folder was also an added directory and permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories was on
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a session failing to start when a rate limit (HTTP 429, or a git wrapper that exits 75) blocks an added read-only repository; it now starts without that repository
  • Improved startup time for Pro and Max accounts by skipping two network requests on launches within an hour of the last check
  • Improved /teleport and claude --teleport to warn when a compacted cloud session loads from its last compaction, so the messages it summarized aren't in the local copy
  • Improved the messages shown when a background session's process exits: they no longer promise a restart that isn't coming, and they say how to resume the session
  • Improved artifacts with several views: Claude now routes each view on the link's #name and no longer says the address bar stays the same as you switch views
  • Improved shell commands that reach their timeout: the result now shows the output so far and says the command is still running in the background
  • Improved compaction: when the model's reply has no summary in it, Claude Code now usually asks for the summary once more before it replaces the conversation
  • Improved the Artifact tool's choice between a page and a document: explainers and visual or interactive work become artifact pages; documents are for writing people keep editing or pass around
  • Improved startup time for launches whose only arguments are options and their values, such as claude --model opus
  • Improved the "Connection dropped" API error: it now says where to look first (the proxy or gateway in use, else VPN or firewall; Anthropic API only, Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry are unchanged)
  • Improved screen reader mode: deleting a rule in /permissions says "Deleted allow rule …" right away
  • Improved the message shown when a pasted sign-in code is refused: it now says the code may have expired or been used, and to sign in again
  • Improved Slack connector sends: Claude now checks a channel's topic for posting rules before messaging a channel you didn't name
  • Improved screen reader mode: Claude's questions are listed as "Questions: Color (answered), Pages", without arrows or symbols
  • Changed ultrathink in the interactive terminal to run its turn at xhigh effort on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.1 through Anthropic's API; typed while Claude is working, it raises the rest of that turn
  • Changed the ultrathink rainbow to appear only where the keyword can raise effort, and not when the word is quoted or part of a file path
  • Changed Ctrl+D in agent view to match the prompt: on an empty input, pressing it twice exits
  • Changed --output-format json and stream-json output to write DEL, C1 control and Unicode format characters inside strings as \uXXXX escapes; parsed values are unchanged
  • Changed model names and IDs to drop the [1m] suffix and its label on models where the suffix has no effect; the suffix is still accepted
  • Changed startup warnings about permission rules in settings files to show once per user until the rule changes
  • Changed /code-review to tell Claude to put the effort level first and use max only when asked
  • Changed DISABLE_COMPACT in settings files and in a mod's $.env.set so they can only turn compaction off, not back on
  • Changed Claude Code on Bedrock, Mantle, Vertex, and Foundry to load model settings from a signed file on downloads.claude.ai; set CLAUDE_CODE_MODEL_CATALOG=off to turn this off
  • Changed sessions that set CLAUDE_CODE_SYNC_SKILLS with feature-flag fetching off to reuse a claude.ai skills list up to 10 minutes old that another session on the machine fetched
  • Changed clicks on scrollbar arrows and bars in fullscreen lists to act when the mouse button is released, so moving off the scrollbar before letting go cancels the click
  • Changed claude purge to say it deletes data only on this computer, not anything stored by Anthropic
  • [VSCode] Added syntax coloring to code blocks in Claude's replies, in light, dark and high contrast dark themes
  • [VSCode] Added a "Running UserPromptSubmit hooks" spinner status and screen reader announcement for slow UserPromptSubmit hooks
  • [VSCode] Fixed custom skills and custom slash commands sent from the VS Code or JetBrains panel leaving out the open file or selected lines that ordinary messages include (#102799)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the extension host freezing while the login shell ran its start-up files to read PATH on macOS and Linux
  • [VSCode] Fixed clicking an image in a tool result, or closing its preview, also opening the result's text in an editor tab
  • [VSCode] Fixed voice dictation continuing to record after a message was sent with the Send button; sending now stops dictation first, as pressing Enter already did
  • [VSCode] Changed the extension to start Claude Code sessions with DISABLE_TELEMETRY set while VS Code's telemetry setting is off, so they send no usage metrics or error reports and fetch no feature flags
  • [VSCode] Changed the session list side bar to load Web sessions when the Web tab is first opened, not at startup
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed routines in Anthropic-hosted environments staying locked after their owner left the organization and rejoined; the owner can now turn them back on
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed routine API token delete or regenerate showing nothing if the edit dialog had already closed; it now shows an error toast
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed cloud environment dialogs, including the admin dialog, accepting duplicate names; they now refuse a name another listed environment already has
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Skills view to Claude Tag analytics showing how often Claude runs each attached skill in Slack channels and which go unused, with Usage links in admin settings
  • [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag routines that run in a new session: a run with nothing to report can now end without posting a throwaway message to the channel
  • [Claude Tag] Changed Claude Tag admin settings to show a lock instead of # for private Slack channels that your own Slack account can see
  • [Code Review] Improved Code Review's check run to say no further automatic review will start when the model still can't analyze a change on the automatic retry
  • [Code Review] Improved Code Review reliability: a review whose session fails to start because of a transient server fault is now retried once automatically, and its check run says so

title: Innovate on your own business terms: Google Cloud spend caps now generally available
summary:
Today, we’re announcing that spend caps on Google Cloud Budgets are generally available. 

With this release, we’re delivering ways to protect your workloads from runaway costs without risking resource deletion. More importantly, we’re introducing three major updates, directly inspired by your feedback since the initial preview, to bring programmability, real-time visibility, and automated guardrails to your cost-control playbook.

How the new spend caps can help your business 

We have significantly enhanced the usability and power of spend caps in three ways: 

1. Automation through spend caps API: Managing guardrails manually across hundreds of projects is a major operational challenge. To address this, we have launched the spend caps API, which can be accessed from the existing Cloud Billing Budgets API. You can now programmatically enforce your financial boundaries for eligible services within each project, without additional overhead. You can automatically lift, update, or delete caps on the fly and instantly apply a spend cap whenever a developer spins up a new sandbox project.

2. Real-time visibility with live cost reports: Spend caps for AI services trigger within minutes of usage using estimated, live costs. When a cap triggers, you need to know exactly why and when the limit was breached. You can now view these faster, estimated costs directly inside your Cost Reports. Instead of waiting hours for standard billing pipelines to settle net costs, you get the exact financial snapshots that triggered the enforcement, giving you the immediate context needed to run a precise root-cause analysis.

3. Automated guardrails for your monthly resets: Before, once a spend cap was triggered, the usage block remained locked until you manually lifted it in the UI. Today, we are introducing automated monthly resets. You no longer need to worry about manually lifting caps every month. Enforced spend caps will automatically reset, and blocked services will seamlessly resume at the beginning of the next month. However, if your governance policies require a strict manual audit before resuming operations, the manual override option continues to exist exactly as before. 

Best practices for deploying spend caps

As you roll out spend caps across your organization, keep these operational tips in mind:

  1. Target non-production environments first: Start by applying strict, low-dollar spend caps to your developer sandboxes, testing clusters, and experimental AI agent playgrounds.
  2. Configure alerts wisely: Default alerts are automatically sent to billing administrators and project owners at 50%, 80%, and 100% of the cap. Make sure the right folks are set up in these roles. This ensures your team is never caught off guard when a budget is nearing depletion. Spend caps permissions can also be added to custom roles, if needed.  
  3. Understand fixed vs on-demand costs: Spend caps halt pay-as-you-go and CUD-covered requests once the budget threshold is hit. However, Provisioned Throughput is never halted; requests using reserved capacity will continue to run, and serve traffic normally.

Refresher on GCP’s dual-pronged defense playbook

Spend Caps work seamlessly alongside our native Early Anomalies Detection to provide a closed-loop defense for your cloud spend. Read our previous blog for a detailed explanation on how to use these tools to effortlessly set up a GCP defense playbook.

Get started today

Spend caps are now ready to support your workloads at scale. Read our documentation for more details and navigate to the Budgets and Alerts page in your Google Cloud Billing Console, to set your first spend cap. 

To integrate programmatic guardrails into your deployment workflows, check out our newly published spend caps API documentation.
